summary: Specifies how DNS can store E.164 telephone numbers and find services tied to a number. It brings ENUM in line with the Dynamic Delegation Discovery System, and obsoletes RFC 2916. It must be read alongside the documents described in RFC 3401. It was replaced by RFC 6116 and RFC 6117.

plainLanguage.summary: This turns a phone number into a special internet name, so a lookup can tell you how else to reach that person.

questions: how to look up phone numbers in dns
subtitle: How a telephone number is turned into a DNS name and used to find the services reachable at that number.

tldr.problem: Given an E.164 telephone number, there was a need to find, in a decentralized way, which services (and which URIs) are connected to that number.
tldr.mechanism: The number is turned into a domain name under e164.arpa by removing non-digits, separating digits with dots, reversing them and appending the suffix. NAPTR records at that name hold rewrite rules that produce a URI.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3761 obsoleted RFC 2916 to align ENUM with the DDDS specifications, and was itself replaced by RFC 6116 and RFC 6117.

today: RFC 3761 is obsolete: it was replaced by RFC 6116 and RFC 6117. It had itself obsoleted RFC 2916.

sections.title: ENUM and the e164.arpa Tree
sections.content:
This document describes how the Domain Name System (DNS) can store E.164 numbers, the international telephone number format, and identify the services available for one number. It obsoletes RFC 2916 to bring it in line with the Dynamic Delegation Discovery System (DDDS) specifications in RFC 3401. The RFC stresses that it is impossible to read and understand it without reading those documents.

By transforming a number into a DNS name and using existing DNS features, namely NS delegation and NAPTR records, a client can look up services in a decentralized way with distributed management at each level. The domain e164.arpa is divided into subdomains, and holders of E.164 numbers who want to be listed contact the zone administrator under that zone's policy, which may differ in different parts of the world.

The same mechanisms might be used for private dialing plans, but then the suffix MUST NOT be e164.arpa and the use MUST NOT be called "ENUM".
sections.plainLanguage: The phone system and the internet each have their own address books. ENUM is a way to look a phone number up in the internet's address book and find other ways to reach it.

sections.title: From Phone Number to DNS Name
sections.content:
The Application Unique String is the fully qualified E.164 number with every non-digit removed except a leading +. The First Well Known Rule is the identity rule, so its output is the same string. ENUM is only for E.164 numbers, and clients MUST only query DNS for what they believe is an E.164 number.

To build the DNS key, the string is converted in four steps: remove everything but the digits, put dots between the digits, reverse their order, and append .e164.arpa. The NAPTR records found at that name may hold the end result or, when the flags field is blank, produce new keys to look up.

The only flag defined is U, meaning the rule is the last one and its output is a URI. A client that meets an unknown flag MUST ignore that record and move to the next rule. The ENUM algorithm always returns a single rule. The Order field in a NAPTR is a request from the number holder that clients MUST follow, while Preference is only a suggestion the client may take under advisement.
sections.plainLanguage: You write the phone number backwards with dots between the digits and add a special ending. That gives you an internet name where the answers are kept.

sections.title: The Service Field
sections.content:
The Service field of a NAPTR record has the form E2U followed by one or more Enumservices, each introduced by a +. An Enumservice is a type plus optional subtypes separated by :, and the type and each subtype are 1 to 32 letters or digits. The E2U part marks ENUM-only rewrite rules, which mitigates collisions between E.164 and non-E.164 numbers.

An Enumservice specification says what it can be used for, the valid protocols and the URI schemes that may be returned. There is no implicit mapping between the textual type and any URI scheme or protocol, so any mapping must be stated in the specification. Types and subtypes used for experiments start with X- and are unregistered.

This format is one of two major changes from RFC 2916. The old service format was example+E2U and the new one is E2U+example. The other major change is that the document now uses the explicit DDDS algorithm, which the RFC says implies no change in the deployed base of applications.
sections.plainLanguage: Each answer carries a label saying what kind of contact it is, such as a voice call or a message, so your software can pick the one it understands.

sections.title: Registering New Enumservices
sections.content:
Enumservices are registered with IANA using the type as the main key. A complete registration includes the allowed subtypes and URI schemes, a functional specification, security considerations and intended usage. It requires IESG approval and publication as an RFC, either on the Standards Track, Experimental, or as a BCP.

A registered Enumservice MUST specify the URI scheme or schemes it may use. Its type MUST be unique, MUST fit the ABNF and MUST NOT start with X-. A subtype must be unique within its type. A security analysis is required for every registration, and a claim of "no security issues" must not be confused with issues that have not been assessed.

Registrations may not be deleted. An Enumservice that is no longer appropriate can be declared OBSOLETE by a new RFC. The registration template lists the intended usage as one of COMMON, LIMITED USE or OBSOLETE.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone who wants a new kind of contact label has to write it up properly and get it approved, so labels mean the same thing everywhere.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content:
The RFC gives a zone with three records for the domain 3.8.0.0.6.9.2.3.6.1.4.4.e164.arpa. All are terminal rules using the u flag and the regular expression !^.*$!. The Order field is 10 in each and the Preference values are 100, 101 and 102.

The records mean the number is preferably contacted by SIP, secondly by H.323 for voice, and thirdly by SMTP for messaging. The tokens sip, h323 and msg are Types registered with IANA and have no implicit link to protocols or URI schemes with the same names. The next step is to use the resolution mechanism of each URI scheme (sip, h323, mailto) to find which node to contact. The RFC notes the services in the examples are theoretical.
sections.plainLanguage: The example is like a contact card for one number listing three ways to reach it: first by video or voice call, then another call system, then a message.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
ENUM relies on DNS, which in its current form gives no way to confirm that returned data is authentic, so attacking the DNS is one way to attack ENUM. The RFC lists threats taken from a DNS threat analysis: packet interception, ID guessing and query prediction, name-based attacks, betrayal by a trusted server, denial of service, and authenticated denial of domain names. Missing records could even be used to change call routing policy.

A deployed ENUM service SHOULD include mitigations. Most threats can be addressed by verifying data with DNSSEC, but denial of service cannot be solved by data authentication, and a service should still authenticate its peers rather than blindly trust any addressing mechanism. ENUM software MUST be prepared to receive DNSSEC and other standardized DNS security responses, including large responses and EDNS0 signaling.

Caching means a change takes as long as the NAPTR time to live to propagate. Where several providers offer call routing, there must be adequate identification, authentication and authorization of those requesting changes. Security issues of the URIs themselves belong in each Enumservice registration.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the lookup uses the ordinary internet address book, a trickster could slip in a fake answer. Using signed answers helps, but you should still check you are really talking to the right person.
